White vs. Black: The First-Move Advantage

White wins 52.34% of decisive games (10,001 of 19,108), compared with Black's 47.66%. That is a +2.34 percentage-point edge over parity. A normal approximation binomial test against 50/50 gives z = 6.47 and p = 9.97e-11; the 95% confidence interval for White's decisive win rate is 51.63%–53.05%.

Centerpiece result: the first-move edge is positive in aggregate, but it is modest in practical terms—roughly 2.3 extra White wins per 100 decisive games relative to exact parity.

Rating Dynamics and Their Impact on Outcomes

Rating differential is the strongest outcome signal in the dataset. Among decisive, non-equal-rating games, the higher-rated player wins 65.3% of the time. The Pearson correlation between absolute rating gap and higher-rated-player win indicator is 0.229, but the binned view below is more informative than the single coefficient.

Conversion curve: when rating gaps are only 0–49 points, the higher-rated player wins 51.6% of decisive games; at 800+, that rises to 94.6%.

Opening Analysis: Popular Openings and Their Success Rates

Opening coverage is highly fragmented, so this section focuses on the top 15 exact opening names by frequency. The most common opening is Van't Kruijs Opening (A00) with 368 games and a White decisive win rate of 35.8%.

Openings where Black outperforms White among the top 15: Van't Kruijs Opening (A00, black 64.2%); Sicilian Defense: Bowdler Attack (B20, black 58.0%); Scandinavian Defense (B01, black 57.7%); Philidor Defense #2 (C41, black 51.9%); Indian Game (A45, black 59.2%); Sicilian Defense (B50, black 53.4%); Owen Defense (B00, black 52.2%); King's Pawn Game: Wayward Queen Attack (C20, black 53.2%); Sicilian Defense: Old Sicilian (B30, black 60.8%).

Key Findings and Strategic Takeaways

White has a real but narrow edge. White scores 52.34% of decisive games, a +2.34 pp margin over parity. Analysts should treat color as a meaningful control variable, not as the dominant predictor.
Rating gap drives conversion. The higher-rated player wins 65.3% of decisive non-equal-rating games, and the binned curve climbs from 51.6% at 0–49 to 94.6% at 800+.
Time pressure changes failure modes. Bullet (≤2m) has the highest timeout share (15.3%), so training and platform analysis should separate tactical quality from clock-management effects.
Openings should be evaluated by sample size. The top-opening table highlights only frequent openings; within those, Black leads in: Van't Kruijs Opening (A00, black 64.2%); Sicilian Defense: Bowdler Attack (B20, black 58.0%); Scandinavian Defense (B01, black 57.7%); Philidor Defense #2 (C41, black 51.9%); Indian Game (A45, black 59.2%); Sicilian Defense (B50, black 53.4%); Owen Defense (B00, black 52.2%); King's Pawn Game: Wayward Queen Attack (C20, black 53.2%); Sicilian Defense: Old Sicilian (B30, black 60.8%).
Game length is outcome-sensitive. The dataset average is 60.5 turns, but length varies by rating tier, ending type, and time control; using only aggregate turns can mask these interactions.
Practical coaching implication. Pair opening preparation with rating-gap expectations: when players are closely matched, small color/opening edges matter more; at large rating gaps, conversion skill dominates.

Methodology and Limitations

  • Primary source: every statistic and chart is computed from /app/benchmark/data.csv.
  • White win rate KPI: calculated as White wins divided by White plus Black wins, excluding draws as specified.
  • Rating brackets: based on the average of White and Black ratings in each game; rating-differential bins use white_rating - black_rating.
  • Time-control families: derived from base minutes in increment_code: bullet ≤2, blitz 3–8, rapid 10–25, classical/long >25.
  • Opening analysis limitation: exact opening_name values are fragmented by variation; this report prioritizes the top 15 exact names by frequency and does not claim coverage of every ECO family.
  • Statistical limitation: the report is descriptive and observational; it identifies associations, not causal effects.
